Record B keeps in place universal, free tax-funded health coverage for every resident and a far stronger income floor (about 50 percent of median income versus about 6 percent), and it enacted further expansions such as abolishing the two-child benefit limit, whereas Record A defends a system that leaves about 8 percent of residents uninsured and guarantees only a minimal income floor.

Record B keeps universal no-charge health coverage and a universal pension in place, opposed health cuts, and voted to raise the minimum pension, so it supports guarantees on both health and income; Record A's strong single-plan bill covers health only, while the income support it keeps in place stays minimal.

Record B voted against the cuts to public health coverage and food assistance and for extending the premium subsidies, and it sponsored a universal single-payer health plan, while Record A voted for cuts that reduce coverage and income support.

Record B keeps in place universal compulsory health insurance and much more generous income support (59% unemployment replacement, 39% minimum income guarantee), and its cuts are modest, while Record A keeps a non-universal system and votes for large cuts to low-income health coverage and food assistance, opposing the subsidy extensions.

Both records carry identical official acts, but A adds influence actions that B lacks: a co-led letter opposing cuts to public pensions and health coverage, and a published plan seeking to reverse the coverage cuts and extend prescription cost caps.

Despite enacting some cuts and a stricter basic income benefit, Record A keeps in place universal compulsory health insurance and far stronger income guarantees (a 39% vs 6% minimum income, and higher unemployment replacement), so the overall position it supports is much stronger than Record B's defense of a non-universal system.

The official acts in both records are essentially identical, so the influence items decide it: A's are broader, covering both health and income support (a 208-legislator letter defending public pensions and health coverage, plus a plan to reverse coverage cuts and extend prescription cost caps), while B's influence addresses health only and partly rests its opposition on public debt.

Both records keep the same baseline and vote for the same cuts. Record B goes further against coverage: it pressed for faster and deeper cuts, threatened to block the subsidy extension, and cosponsored a bill to phase down funding for the low-income coverage expansion. That makes Record A the relatively stronger supporter.
